title: Wisdom for every day (Proverbs 9:10; Sirach 6:14)
hookLine: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; a faithful friend is a strong defense

cards: Proverbs chapter nine sets up two dinner invitations. The first comes from Wisdom, pictured as a woman. In the Douay-Rheims: "Wisdom hath built herself a house, she hath hewn her out seven pillars."
She's slaughtered the meat, mixed the wine, set the table, and sent her maids to call from the tower and the walls of the city: whoever is a little one, come in here.
Across town, another woman, called Folly, sits at her own door and calls out to the same people walking by, almost word for word. Same street. Same passersby.

teach.h: FEAR OF THE LORD: AWE, NOT TERROR.
teach.b: Between the two invitations is the line the whole book of Proverbs leans on: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." Fear here isn't terror. It's closer to awe, the reverence that knows God is God and I'm not.
Catholics count fear of the Lord among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, from the Isaiah passage a couple of weeks ago. Wisdom starts there, and then it gets very practical.
Which brings in a second wisdom book, one that's in Catholic Bibles: Sirach, also called Ecclesiasticus, not to be confused with yesterday's Ecclesiastes.

Its writer signs it near the end: Jesus son of Sirach, of Jerusalem. A prologue says his grandson carried it into Greek in Egypt, with an apology: things said in Hebrew lose some of their force in another language.
In chapter six he talks about friends with real street sense.
Some are friends for their own convenience and won't stay in the day of your trouble. Some sit at your table and vanish when things go bad. Test a friend before you trust him.
And then: "A faithful friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found him, hath found a treasure."
Nothing can be weighed against a faithful friend, he adds; such a friend is medicine for life.

Look back at this week: Micah's careful walk, Jonah running and sulking, Job's friends sitting silent, the whirlwind, the seasons, and now wisdom in a friend. A week of learning to live with God and with each other.

how: Catholics hear Proverbs and Sirach in the Mass readings, especially on weekdays, and the Church counts fear of the Lord among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit received in confirmation.

o: the writer of Ecclesiastes, called Qoheleth
a wisdom book found in Catholic Bibles
a prophet who preached to the exiles

games.q: two wisdom books — tap the pairs.
p: Sirach, by Jesus son of Sirach

s: Ecclesiasticus and Ecclesiastes are the same book
Ecclesiastes is Qoheleth; Ecclesiasticus is Sirach, written by Jesus son of Sirach.
the fear of the Lord in Proverbs means being terrified of God
it's closer to awe and reverence, and Catholics count it among the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
Sirach says to test a friend before you trust him
try him before thou takest him, he says; some friends are companions at the table and won't abide in the day of distress.

games.q: you're walking through town. Wisdom calls from her house of seven pillars: come in. a few doors down, Folly calls you with almost the same words. what do you do?
o: go wherever the louder voice is.
games.why: both invitations sound alike; Proverbs says the difference begins with the fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom.

practice: Think of a friend who stayed in the day of your trouble, if one comes to mind: the one who was there when it went bad.
Remember one specific thing they did, a phone call, a ride, a long silence beside you, a hard truth told kindly, and let gratitude come. If you pray, thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Sirach. The wisdom book, also called Ecclesiasticus, that says a faithful friend is a strong defense and a treasure beyond price. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: fear, awe, reverence, as in the fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom.

carryVoice: Your line: a friend is treasure. Two open doors, and one good friend. Day four hundred thirty-four, and a full week.
